reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive dystrophy, most often reported in Japanese populations, presenting in the first two decades with severe photophobia, tearing, and progressive visual loss
Caused by mutations in the TACSTD2 gene (encoding tumour-associated calcium signal transducer 2), which disrupts corneal epithelial tight junctions
Subepithelial amyloid accumulates as mulberry-like gelatinous nodules that raise and opacify the corneal surface
The amyloid deposits stain with Congo red and show characteristic birefringence, similar to lattice dystrophy but located subepithelially
Loss of the epithelial barrier increases permeability and drives progressive amyloid deposition, causing marked visual impairment relatively early
The band-keratopathy-like and mulberry appearances distinguish it from the stromal lattice dystrophies
Management includes lubrication and surface care, with superficial keratectomy, phototherapeutic keratectomy, or lamellar/penetrating keratoplasty, though recurrence is common
Deposits characteristically recur rapidly on the surface after removal because of the persistent barrier defect
reference.pathophysiology: Gelatinous drop-like corneal dystrophy is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the TACSTD2 gene, which encodes a protein important for corneal epithelial tight junction integrity. Loss of normal tight junctions markedly increases epithelial permeability, allowing serum-derived proteins to enter the subepithelial cornea where they aggregate as amyloid. The resulting mulberry-like gelatinous subepithelial nodules progressively opacify and elevate the surface, causing severe photophobia and visual loss from an early age. The underlying barrier defect drives rapid re-accumulation of amyloid after surgical removal.
additionalDifferentials: Lattice corneal dystrophy and other stromal amyloid deposition
Polymorphic amyloid degeneration secondary to chronic surface disease
Superficial scarring from severe ocular surface disease
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy showing mulberry-like subepithelial nodules
Histology with Congo red staining confirming subepithelial amyloid
TACSTD2 genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography to map subepithelial deposits
In vivo confocal microscopy of the epithelial and subepithelial layers
Assessment of epithelial barrier function and surface staining
redFlags: Severe early visual loss from confluent subepithelial amyloid
Rapid recurrence of deposits after surgical removal
Secondary infection of a compromised, highly permeable surface
reference.prognosis: The disorder tends to cause severe visual impairment from an early age and is more visually aggressive than the classic stromal amyloid dystrophies. Surgery can temporarily improve vision, but deposits recur rapidly because of the persistent epithelial barrier defect, often requiring repeated intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking subepithelial amyloid nodules for band keratopathy or Salzmann degeneration
Expecting durable benefit from superficial keratectomy despite rapid recurrence
Overlooking the autosomal recessive inheritance and family risk
Failing to recognise the epithelial barrier defect underlying the disease
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Superficial keratectomy to remove mulberry-like subepithelial amyloid and improve vision, with the expectation of rapid recurrence from the persistent epithelial barrier defect
Lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty for severe visual loss, monitoring for recurrent deposition within the graft
Rigid contact lens wear as a protective barrier to reduce the rate of amyloid re-accumulation after surgery
Symptomatic relief of severe photophobia, tearing and foreign-body sensation with lubricants and tinted lenses
Anterior segment imaging and slit-lamp follow-up to map deposits and detect recurrence for timely re-intervention
Confirm the amyloid is localised to the cornea without systemic involvement
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive TACSTD2 inheritance and testing of at-risk family members
